inventory.visualPurpose: The 'Challenging patient and ethical scenarios' table, page one (book 274): the lead-in (appropriate responses are patient-centered, open-ended, and empathetic — acknowledge obstacles, validate emotions, create open-ended dialogue; reflect autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice; consider patient, family, culture, and healthcare team points of view) plus 13 SITUATION/APPROPRIATE RESPONSE rows, from 'Patient does not follow the medical plan.' through 'Patient is upset with treatment received from another physician.' — the Communication Skills subsection's situation-response dictionary, part one
inventory.sourceFigureDescription: COLOR-CODED TABLE, no raster (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM-read at 120dpi, staging-pubh24/vlm-census.txt — VLM available this session): the running header (274 / SECTION II / PUBLIC HEALTH SCIENCES / '▶ PUBLIC HEALTH SCIENCES—COmmUNICATION SkILLS' printed ONCE — running header only, no in-body sub-banner), the bold dark-navy heading 'Challenging patient and ethical scenarios' in a narrow left column with the lead-in paragraph in the right column (the lead-in carries First Aid's signature FIRST-LETTER RED styling on key terms — patient-centered, obstacles, validate, points of view — styling, not a mnemonic), the column headers SITUATION / APPROPRIATE RESPONSE in small bold dark-navy caps over a thin rule, then THIRTEEN rows in printed order with the SITUATION column in regular black roman type, dotted hairline row separators, and NO zebra shading: (1) Patient does not follow the medical plan → determine financial/logistical/other obstacles, do not coerce or refer, schedule regular follow-up; (2) Patient desires an unnecessary procedure → understand why and address underlying concerns, do not refuse to see or refer, avoid performing unnecessary procedures; (3) Patient has difficulty taking medications → determine factors; written instructions, teach-back method, simplified regimens for comprehension/memory issues; (4) Family members ask for information about patient's prognosis → avoid discussing with relatives without the patient's permission; (5) Family member asks you not to disclose results if prognosis is poor ('unable to handle it') → explore why incl. cultural factors; information not withheld if the patient wants it; therapeutic privilege only if the patient might seriously harm self or others; (6) A 17-year-old is pregnant and requests an abortion → many states require parental notification/consent; do not sway the decision; discuss options and refer to abortion care; (7) A 15-year-old is pregnant and wants to raise the child (parents want adoption) → the patient retains the right to make decisions regarding the child; practical information; discuss termination options if requested; encourage patient-parent discussion; (8) A terminally ill patient requests physician-assisted dying → most states prohibit; medically appropriate analgesics permitted even if they potentially shorten life; (9) Patient is suicidal → assess seriousness; voluntary hospitalization suggested, involuntary if needed; (10) Patient states you are attractive and asks for a date → chaperone if necessary; romantic relationships never appropriate; firm boundaries; transition care if necessary; (11) A woman post-mastectomy feels 'ugly' → find out why; no falsely reassuring statements ('You still look good'); (12) Patient is angry about waiting-room time → acknowledge, do not take personally, thank and apologize, stay away from explaining the delay; (13) Patient is upset with treatment from another physician → suggest speaking directly to that physician; office-staff problems handled by you. NO mnemonics, margin notes, asterisk footnotes, images, or icons anywhere on the page (VLM-explicit).

inventory.visualPurpose: The 'Challenging patient and ethical scenarios (continued)' table, page two (book 275): the final 12 SITUATION/APPROPRIATE RESPONSE rows, from 'An invasive test is performed on the wrong patient.' through 'A pediatrician recommends standard vaccinations for a patient, but the child's parent refuses.' — the error-disclosure, coverage, bereaved-child, intimate-partner-violence, alternative-medicine, impaired-colleague, brain-death, sponsorship, conscience, Jehovah's Witness, abuse-reporting, and vaccine-refusal rows; the table ends on this page
inventory.sourceFigureDescription: COLOR-CODED TABLE, no raster (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM-read at 120dpi, staging-pubh24/vlm-census.txt — VLM available this session): the running header (PUBLIC HEALTH SCIENCES / '▶ PUBLIC HEALTH SCIENCES—COmmUNICATION SkILLS' / SECTION II / 275), the bold dark-blue continuation title 'Challenging patient and ethical scenarios (continued)' ('(continued)' bold italic) over a thin rule, the repeated column headers SITUATION / APPROPRIATE RESPONSE in small bold dark-blue caps, then TWELVE rows in printed order (SITUATION column regular black; thin rules between rows; no zebra shading; no red text in any cell): (14) An invasive test is performed on the wrong patient → regardless of outcome, ethically obligated to inform the patient a mistake has been made; (15) A patient requires a treatment not covered by insurance → discuss all treatment options even if uncovered; inform of financial assistance programs; (16) A 7-year-old boy loses a sister to cancer and now feels responsible → at ages 5-7 children understand death is permanent; direct concrete description; avoid clichés and euphemisms; reassure he is not responsible; identify and normalize fears; encourage play and healthy coping; (17) Patient is victim of intimate partner violence → ask if safe, devise emergency plan; direct open-ended questions; summarize answers back; do not necessarily pressure to leave partner or disclose to authorities (unless required by state law); (18) Patient wants to try alternative or holistic medicine → explore underlying reasons supportively and nonjudgmentally; advise benefits/risks incl. interactions; consider referral to a CAM provider; (19) Physician colleague presents to work impaired → risk to patient safety; ethical and usually legal obligation to report; seek guidance as procedures/law vary; (20) Family insists on life support after brain death, citing patient's movements → gently explain no chance of recovery; brain death is equivalent to death; movement is spinal arc reflex, not voluntary; bring case to ethics board re futility; (21) A pharmaceutical company offers a sponsorship to advertise its new drug → reject; generally decline gifts/sponsorships to avoid conflict of interest; AMA Code of Ethics exceptions (gifts directly benefitting patients; medical-education funding for students/residents/fellows; independent-criteria grants; unattributed funds); (22) Patient requests a nonemergent procedure against your personal or religious beliefs → provide accurate unbiased information; explain neutrally you do not perform it; offer to refer; (23) Mother and 15-year-old daughter unresponsive and bleeding heavily, father refuses transfusion (Jehovah's Witnesses) → transfuse daughter, but do not transfuse mother; proxy may refuse emergent care for an adult when preferences known/reasonably inferred, but not for a minor based solely on faith; (24) A dependent patient presents with injuries inconsistent with caretaker's story → document detailed H&P; interview alone if possible; provide care; contact agencies/authorities (child or adult protective services) if suspicion remains; inform caretaker of obligation; physicians required by law to report any reasonable suspicion of abuse, neglect, or endangerment; (25) A pediatrician recommends standard vaccinations but the child's parent refuses → address concerns; explain risks/benefits and why recommended; do not administer routine vaccinations without the parent's consent. The table ENDS at this row with a closing horizontal rule (VLM-confirmed; no third page). The FINAL row interleaves its two cells line-by-line in the raw text layer — documented quirk; the VLM read confirms the clean two-cell reading. NO mnemonics, margin notes, asterisk footnotes, images, or icons anywhere on the page (VLM-explicit).

notes: The topic carries TWO visual assets — the book-274 'Challenging patient and ethical scenarios' table part (sv1: lead-in + 13 rows, from 'Patient does not follow the medical plan.' through 'Patient is upset with treatment received from another physician.') and the book-275 '(continued)' table part (sv2: the final 12 rows, from 'An invasive test is performed on the wrong patient.' through the vaccine-refusal row where the table ENDS with a closing rule) — both accounted for as ORIGINAL KYP ADAPTATIONS: nothing is reproduced; ONE registry visual (challenging-scenarios-map, ChallengingScenariosMap in visuals/pubhealth-p24.tsx, viewBox 0 0 1102 1380) rebuilds the two-page table as original KYP vector art — the lead-in triad band (patient-centered · open-ended · empathetic with the three printed example phrases and the principles + lenses strips), SEVEN themed cluster cards (adherence barriers · consent & disclosure · minors · end-of-life & loss · boundaries & professionalism · safety & reporting · conflicts of interest & conscience) carrying ALL 25 situations with the verbatim key phrases of their responses, and the override-threshold rule strip — deliberately NOT a 25-row wall; both pages' full text is additionally carried verbatim in the note's two table blocks. Census: zero raster images on both pages (pdfimages); VLM available this session — TWO 120dpi full-page glm-4.6v passes (vlm-census.txt) confirmed the printed row order and counts of both pages (13 + 12 = 25, none missing or extra), every response cell verbatim, the lead-in and its three quoted example phrases, the dotted hairlines and absence of zebra shading, the regular-black SITUATION column, the once-only banner on 296, and the absence of mnemonics, margin notes, red in-cell text, asterisk footnotes, images, and icons. ADJUDICATIONS (all reads agree unless noted): ROW COUNT — the batch brief's '24-row' is a miscount; the print carries 25 rows (13 + 12), and the chapter census's own productionRationale enumerates 25 situations — print governs, all 25 carried; the VLM's 'spinal are reflex' in the brain-death row is a 120dpi misread adjudicated to the text layer's 'spinal arc reflex'; the FINAL row (vaccines) interleaves its two cells line-by-line in the raw text layer — the inventory and note carry the de-interleaved reading (VLM-confirmed); the lead-in's first-letter red styling is First Aid's signature styling, not a mnemonic — no FA-own mnemonic prints anywhere on either page (VLM-explicit).
